Abstract of Praxis
Identifying Autonomous AI APT

Autonomous artificial intelligence agents can perform cybersecurity actions, but distinguishing their behavior from human-operated activity remains sensitive to environment and collection method. This Praxis proposes a matched laboratory study of defender-visible host and network features during APT-like activity. Human red-team participants and autonomous agents will pursue equivalent objectives over five collection days using a published AWS range design. The intended external AI controller is an NVIDIA DGX Spark running locally supplied Gemma and Qwen variants. Command diversity and command-sequence transition entropy are the principal hypothesized features. Logistic regression will test transfer to unseen groups; support vector machines, trees, random forests, XGBoost and a tabular transformer will be compared under common grouped evaluation. EDA will assess completeness, dependence, feature stability and collection shortcuts. Trial-level macro-F1 is primary; false AI labels on humans, class recall, balanced accuracy, calibration and cost provide supporting evidence.

ILLUSTRATIVE OUTCOME ONLY: A capacity example assumes 120 primary trials and 24 controls, including 40 locked primary trials. An invented SVM confusion matrix yields macro-F1 of 0.825 and a human false-AI rate of 0.150. These values demonstrate reporting; they are not findings or forecasts with validated uncertainty. Formal hypothesis decisions remain pending.

The intended contribution is a reproducible attribution protocol with explicit provenance and transfer limits. Positive, negative and inconclusive outcomes are possible; operator attribution is distinct from intrusion detection and geopolitical attribution.

text: Chapter 1 Introduction
1.1 Background

Defenders observe intrusion effects without necessarily knowing whether a person or autonomous agent selected each action. Process creation, authentication and network connections offer possible behavioral evidence. However, humans, scripts and AI agents can use the same tools. Attribution requires controlled comparisons rather than treating rapid activity or one executable as proof of AI control. Alt (2026) examined automation classes in SSH interactions, while Ediga and Chattopadhyay (2026) examined AI-family terminal fingerprints. These motivate, but do not establish, the present target-side generalization claim.
1.2 Research Motivation

A useful classifier must retain informative patterns when the operator, configuration or collection setting changes. A model that recognizes an archive can appear accurate while failing on another source. The project’s real-record feasibility screen exhibited this problem: within-source performance dropped during transfer, and the two AI sources were highly distinguishable. The practical objective is therefore a bounded assessment of useful features and methods, not an artificially favorable model ranking. Negative findings can identify measurement failures or limits of attribution.
1.3 Problem Statement

It remains uncertain which defender-visible host and network behaviors reliably distinguish human-operated from autonomous-AI APT-like activity in a matched multi-host laboratory, and whether classifiers transfer to unseen operators and AI configurations rather than exploiting collection artifacts.
1.4 Thesis Statement

This study proposes that autonomous AI attacks produce measurable behavioral patterns that distinguish them from human-operated attacks, even when the human operator or AI configuration has not previously been observed. The study will test this proposition using target-side telemetry collected during matched, controlled APT-like laboratory trials.

Alt (2026) and Ediga and Chattopadhyay (2026) provide supporting motivation through automation-class classification and AI-family fingerprinting. Neither demonstrates the full proposed matched autonomous multi-host comparison. The thesis is a proposition for testing.
1.5 Research Objectives

The objectives are to define reproducible target-side features, assess their incremental value, evaluate transfer after timing/tool controls, and compare classifiers under common information and tuning limits. Supporting outputs include a provenance-aware data schema, extraction specification and reproducibility record. Public outputs must not expose credentials or identifiable participant information.
1.6 Research Questions and Hypotheses
RQ1: Which target-side host and network behavioral feature families distinguish human-operated from autonomous-AI APT-like trials under matched conditions?
H1: Command diversity and command-sequence transition entropy improve classification of human-operated versus autonomous-AI APT-like activity compared with a predefined baseline.
RQ2: Which classifiers retain useful behavioral attributes for classification performance on autonomous-AI APT data?
H2: Logistic regression retains useful behavioral attributes and achieves above-baseline classification performance on previously unseen autonomous-AI configurations and human operators.
RQ3: Among XGBoost, a decision tree, a random forest, SVM and a tabular transformer, which provides the strongest trial-level human-versus-autonomous-AI classification?
H3: SVM achieves higher trial-level macro-F1 than XGBoost, a decision tree, a random forest and a tabular transformer for human-versus-autonomous-AI classification.

These hypotheses were approved October 24, 2026 after exploratory analysis. They are not retrospective preregistrations; formal data must supply a separate evaluation. Lack of support does not prove equality, and the largest point estimate alone does not support H3.
1.7 Scope of Research

The population is authorized attack trials on a controlled range. APT-like denotes staged objectives and persistence within the exercise, not attribution to a real threat organization. Benign and scripted controls remain separate. A binary model trained on attack trials is not a general intrusion detector. External controller placement describes the network boundary, not unrestricted Internet targeting.

The author supplied huihui_ai/qwen2.5-coder-abliterate:32b, local identifier 36711483afce, displayed size 19 GB; and gemma4-ablit:latest, local identifier 63f914bef7f4, displayed size 16 GB. These entries identify intended artifacts but do not verify full digests, base lineage, modifications, capabilities or completed runs.
1.8 Research Limitations

Five days constrain independent-group counts. Multiple windows from one participant or configuration do not create independent subjects. Two checkpoints provide limited family diversity. Prompt holdouts within one checkpoint are configuration transfer, not unseen-family transfer. Boundary latency, task completion and sensor loss may change apparent separability; these limitations must remain visible.
1.9 Organization of Praxis

Chapter 2 reviews prior work and bounds novelty. Chapter 3 specifies the GMR, collection, EDA, algorithms, equations and robustness. Chapter 4 distinguishes actual exploratory findings from illustrative formal-result tables. Chapter 5 develops conditional discussion and conclusions. Appendices define evidence replacement and reproduction requirements.
Chapter 2 Literature Review
2.1 Review Method and Evidence Status

A focused update on October 24, 2026 examined institutional repositories, arXiv, publisher records, official software documentation and GW guidance. Search concepts included human versus autonomous AI attacker classification, terminal behavior fingerprinting, AI honeypot evaluation, matched red-team data and AWS attack ranges. Citation chaining used the existing project review. This is not an exhaustive systematic review with a registered search protocol. Preprints, theses, accepted work and published papers are distinguished, and source metadata inspection is not represented as full-text verification.

Sources were retained when relevant to operator behavior, comparative evaluation, data provenance or the selected algorithms. Unverified news and unrelated prompt-jailbreak benchmarks were not treated as evidence for attribution. The final literature audit must revisit full texts and new publications before claiming priority. No single citation proves novelty.
2.2 Automation Classes and AI Fingerprints

Alt (2026) is the closest direct comparator because it classifies human, conventional automation and AI-assisted activity using SSH honeypot behavior. It prevents a claim that this study is the first to distinguish human and AI-associated sessions. The proposed extension concerns autonomous execution, matched multi-host tasks, defender-side measurement and operator/configuration holdouts. AI-assisted and autonomous labels require different intervention evidence.

Trace attributes AI model families from terminal sequences and reports weaker performance on unseen scaffolds (Ediga & Chattopadhyay, 2026). It makes model-specific fingerprints an explicit concern: a human-versus-AI classifier may learn one implementation rather than a transferable property. Its attribution target differs from the binary operator-type target, but its transfer results motivate scaffold/configuration controls.
2.3 Recent Behavioral and Deception Research

Honey for the Agent examines nine open-weight models across prompts and SSH environments. Its institutional accepted-paper record describes distinctive command-selection fingerprints and effects of environmental cues (Maddaloni et al., in press). It supports feature hypotheses and source-transfer checks but lacks the matched human cohort proposed here. The citation retains its in-press status rather than inventing final pagination.

Honeyquest for LLMs compares models with a human baseline on an identical reconnaissance-query instrument (Prinos et al., 2026). Shared-stimulus human–AI comparisons therefore already exist. Judgment about deception differs from continuous defender-side measurements of live multi-stage activity. The study helps delimit novelty and motivates control of task framing and attacker knowledge.

The September 2026 Rouxii preprint evaluates deception-aware AI pentesters, showing that knowledge and prompting affect their interactions (Cordeiro et al., 2026). This strengthens the requirement to pin prompts and skills. It also cautions against generalizing a classifier from one agent-policy setting to all autonomous attackers. Rouxii does not itself establish the proposed human-versus-AI defender classifier.
2.4 Data and Experimental Infrastructure

GAMBiT provides human red-team cyber-range observations with participant-linked and multimodal records (Beltz et al., 2025). It supports behavior analysis and appropriate grouping of repeated observations. A corresponding 2026 Data in Brief record was located during the update; this draft uses the verified author-complete preprint citation for the experimental description. Different tasks, interventions and environments prevent treating its human traces and unrelated AI archives as a matched study.

Cochise offers a reference planner–executor harness and released trajectories for autonomous penetration-testing research (Happe & Cito, 2026). It is useful as experimental infrastructure and a separate source for feasibility checks. Its controller traces are not native target-side telemetry. The citation does not establish deployment of the intended custom model or AWS topology.

Splunk Attack Range supports reproducible instrumented cloud labs including AWS, with Terraform/Ansible provisioning and optional network visibility (Splunk, n.d.). It is a candidate infrastructure baseline, not evidence of this project’s deployment. Its exact commit, template, modifications and sensors must be recorded to make an implemented range reproducible.
2.5 Models and Evaluation

SVMs learn margin-based separation and can use kernels for nonlinear relationships (Cortes & Vapnik, 1995). Random forests combine randomized trees (Breiman, 2001); XGBoost learns regularized additive trees (Chen & Guestrin, 2016). Their different inductive assumptions should be compared using common information. Tabular benchmark evidence motivates strong tree baselines without guaranteeing a winner in this small grouped study (Grinsztajn et al., 2022). FT-Transformer supplies a concrete numerical-feature comparison, and its authors identify no universally superior family (Gorishniy et al., 2021).

Group-aware validation and training-only preprocessing protect against dependence and leakage. Correlated features can obscure individual permutation importance, making retrained ablation and family-level analysis important companions (scikit-learn developers, n.d.-a, n.d.-b). The earlier project transformer was an FT-style engineering implementation; it remains distinct from a qualified replication of the published baseline.

The candidate contribution is the integration of matched human and autonomous-AI operations, multi-host defender-visible measurement, grouped transfer evaluation, feature ablations and automation controls. Chapter 3 Methodology
3.1 Design and Data Provenance

The study is a proposed controlled matched-trial experiment. A trial is an authorized attempt from a restored range state with an objective, actor, observation budget and outcome record. Events and windows are nested within trials; trials are nested within participants or AI configurations. Human and AI arms receive equivalent access, objectives and allowed tools. Five days describe the collection schedule, not five independent statistical observations.

The project refers to a synthetic dataset because the range and scenario are constructed. For scientific reporting, the manifest will distinguish measured laboratory telemetry, generated synthetic records and illustrative manuscript values. Telemetry produced by real people and agents in the range is real experimental data from a synthetic scenario. The earlier 880-row fixture is generated simulation. The red result tables are manuscript illustrations and do not constitute measured data.

Configuration identity combines checkpoint, scaffold, prompt, skill bundle and inference settings. Configurations from the same checkpoint remain related at the family level. Preserve both IDs. Holding out a prompt or seed does not establish transfer to a new model family. text: 3.3 Graphical Model Representation
Figure 3.2 Graphical model representation of attribution

The GMR is a conceptual directed acyclic graph, not a fitted Bayesian network. Operator type A, task C and environment E influence behavior B. Behavior and measurement conditions generate observations O; features X then support prediction. Sensor quality Q affects what is observable. Environment includes tool/access conditions and can influence both behavior and observation. This makes explicit the route by which a classifier could recognize the environment rather than transferable operator behavior.

Matching C and E reduces systematic arm differences. Canary tests assess Q. Actor/configuration holdouts test recurrence of informative patterns. Timing/tool ablations examine reliance on selected pathways. The graph explains the design but does not identify a causal effect of autonomy from predictive scores. There are no fitted edge weights or causal probabilities to report.

3.6 Exploratory Data Analysis

Begin with label-blind integrity checks. Label-aware feature decisions use development data only; a custodian preserves the locked outcomes. Post-evaluation test plots are descriptive and cannot trigger unreported retuning. The provenance funnel reports scheduled, attempted, logged, valid and excluded trials by arm, group, task and day. Distinguish empty behavior from absent observation and report the number of independent groups.

Summarize duration, event volume, missingness, duplicates, clock error and task success. For numeric features report nonmissing count, median, quartiles, extrema and robust spread. Plot shared-axis histograms or empirical cumulative distributions and stratify by group/task. Do not treat every event as an independent sample. Investigate outliers using provenance rather than removing them because they weaken a hypothesis.

Assess dependence through Spearman correlations and group summaries. Explore relevance using training-fold distributions, univariate discrimination, grouped permutation and retrained ablation. High marginal separation may reflect source; weak marginal separation can coexist with useful interactions. Record inclusion/exclusion reasoning and retain the locked feature definition before final scoring.

text: 3.7 Feature Engineering

The trial is the primary observation. Normalize target-side command/process tokens using a frozen vocabulary, removing identities and assigned experimental cues. Command diversity is distinct tokens divided by observed tokens. Transition entropy summarizes adjacent token-pair frequencies. Both depend on sequence length; report length and repeat analysis on equal-length prefixes. Missing streams do not have zero diversity, and fewer than two tokens cannot define transition entropy.

Process breadth requires validated parent–child events. Network entropy uses protocol observations, while outward traffic fractions require a verified boundary mapping; flow forward/backward fields are not automatically outbound/inbound. Repetition is only a retry proxy unless failed actions and subsequent attempts can be linked. Controller-only statistics cannot silently substitute for target-side features.

3.9 How the Classifiers Work

Logistic regression maps a linear combination of scaled features through a sigmoid to estimate AI probability. Regularization limits coefficient size. Coefficients are conditional model associations, not causal effects. H2 concerns above-baseline transfer after shortcut controls; it does not require logistic regression to win RQ3.

An SVM seeks a separating margin with penalties for violations. C trades margin width against errors, and an RBF kernel permits nonlinear boundaries using distances between scaled features. Gamma determines how local those comparisons are. Raw SVM decision scores are not calibrated probabilities; calibration must use training-only grouped data (Cortes & Vapnik, 1995).

A decision tree recursively selects thresholds that improve node purity. A terminal leaf supplies a class distribution or decision. Depth and leaf-size limits constrain complexity. A random forest averages randomized trees to reduce dependence on one partition (Breiman, 2001). Split-gain importance alone cannot establish H1; held-out ablation is required.

XGBoost adds trees to improve a regularized objective, controlled by learning rate, depth, subsampling and penalties; early stopping observes training-internal validation (Chen & Guestrin, 2016). A tabular transformer embeds numeric features as tokens and learns interactions through attention. It receives the same feature table rather than raw text. The final implementation must be qualified against FT-Transformer (Gorishniy et al., 2021).

3.11 Hypothesis Decision Framework

H1 requires incremental contribution from the named features, not a high overall score. Freeze whether individual and joint benefits are required. H2 tests frozen logistic regression against a declared baseline on unseen groups with reduced features. H3 requires paired evidence that SVM exceeds each of four candidates. A lead in a rounded table is not sufficient. Failed models, ties and inconclusive contrasts remain reportable outcomes.

DRAFT ASSUMPTION: Proposed discussion margins: 0.02 macro-F1 improvement for H1/H3; positive baseline benefit for H2; human false-AI rate no greater than 0.20 as an operational screen. These are provisional targets, not power-justified or institutional criteria. Freeze margins, baselines and adjustment families before final scoring.

A permutation test requires exchangeability at the declared grouped unit; arbitrary label shuffling does not ensure validity. Record pairing, resampling units and whether intervals are descriptive or simultaneous. If the design cannot support reliable inference, limit the conclusion to exploratory estimates. No metric threshold is selected to make the assumed results pass.

text: 3.12 Robustness and Seeding

Robustness removes all timing-derived variables, removes tool names and derived categories, and combines both ablations. Additional analyses restrict command length, hold out tasks or days, and hold out checkpoint families where support exists. Sensor-loss perturbations evaluate random loss and contiguous outages. Shuffled group labels, metadata-only prediction and ordinary automation supply negative controls. Source-recognition models test residual collection differences.

DRAFT ASSUMPTION: Proposed sensor-loss levels: 5%, 10% and 20%, using identical perturbations across candidate models. Proposed bootstrap/permutation counts: 2,000 and 1,000. Formal master seed: 20261024; model repeats: 19, 29, 39, 49, 59. These are unexecuted prospective settings. Illustration tables are hand-specified arithmetic examples, not seeded experimental predictions.

Separate seeds for collection order, partitioning, tuning, fitting, bootstrap, permutation and synthetic generation. Derive component seeds using Equation 31 with UTF-8 encoding and explicit separators. Persist both seed inputs and integers; avoid language-default hash functions. Agent decoding seeds, if supported, are distinct from analysis seeds. Save explicit split manifests rather than trusting a seed to reproduce future library behavior.

Set Python, NumPy and framework RNGs; log deterministic settings and unsupported operations. PyTorch warns that seeds do not guarantee identical results across releases or hardware (PyTorch contributors, n.d.). Preserve package versions, model/tokenizer digests, precision, GPU runtime/driver and thread counts. Computational reproduction reruns identical logs; experimental replication repeats the exercise and is not expected to produce byte-identical human or agent behavior.

Human participation requires the appropriate institutional determination and consent process before collection; approval is not assumed. Restrict activity to authorized range resources and objectives. Credentials and identities remain in restricted evidence; publish sanitized aggregates under appropriate terms. The model artifacts, skills and external route must be auditable. No AWS range or autonomous attack was launched to create this manuscript.

Chapter 4 Results
4.1 Evidence Status

The completed synthetic engineering test and real-archive command screen are exploratory evidence. They are not the planned five-day matched target-side experiment. No formal H1/H2/H3 decision is available. This chapter retains those observed results separately from report-construction examples.

ILLUSTRATIVE RESULTS: Red numbers are invented reporting examples or marked TO COMPUTE. They are not sampling-based estimates or experimental findings. No confidence interval, p-value or hypothesis pass is fabricated.
4.2 Recorded Exploratory Evidence

The real-archive screen used 111 GAMBiT windows from 57 participants, 1,315 Honey windows from nine model identifiers and 38 COCHISE windows from 15 model/configuration identifiers. Ten-command windows and five group-split seeds produced 1,464 real archived observations. These were controller-command records from different studies, not matched target-side trials. Chapter 5 Discussion and Conclusions
5.1 Interpretation Framework

The central question is whether separation reflects behavior under matched conditions or artifacts of the exercise. Strong full-feature performance with weak reduced-feature performance suggests timing/tool reliance. Strong within-configuration performance with weak transfer limits the claim to familiar agents. Frequent AI labels on scripts indicate difficulty separating autonomy from automation. The earlier archive analysis shows why high accuracy alone is inadequate.

Stronger evidence combines held-out discrimination, acceptable human error, stable contributions, independent sensor validation and documented robustness. The matched design reduces source differences but does not guarantee their elimination. A numerical ranking cannot settle these measurement questions.
5.2 Conditional Discussion

ILLUSTRATIVE DISCUSSION FOR REPLACEMENT: In the constructed example, SVM reached macro-F1 0.825, AI recall 0.800 and human false-AI rate 0.150. Such a result would indicate useful but imperfect discrimination in the sampled range. It would not establish superiority without paired uncertainty and corrected comparisons, nor transport to actual adversaries or unseen environments.

CONDITIONAL H1 TEXT: If frozen ablations show supported individual and joint improvements, diversity and entropy can be described as useful predictors in this setting. If only their joint contribution is supported, the conclusion must refer to the combination. If neither helps, report H1 as unsupported instead of substituting a favorable post hoc feature.

CONDITIONAL H2 TEXT: Above-baseline reduced logistic performance on reserved groups would support a bounded transfer claim. Failure on the new checkpoint or removal of timing/tools would instead limit the result. Several prompts from one model do not establish generalization across model families.

CONDITIONAL H3 TEXT: Support requires SVM to exceed every named comparator under the frozen corrected tests. A practical tie may justify choosing a cheaper model but does not support superiority. An unsupported H3 does not invalidate a supported feature finding or transfer result.
5.3 Conclusions

The work currently establishes a research design and auditable reporting structure, not completed evidence that target-side features reliably identify autonomous-AI APT-like activity. Existing exploratory evidence justifies a small matched pilot while demonstrating source-confounding risks. The final conclusion must state what the implemented experiment supports, including a negative or inconclusive outcome.

CONDITIONAL FINAL CONCLUSION: Replace this paragraph with actual sample/group counts, the locked primary score and uncertainty, human false-AI rate, AI recall, transfer limits and the disposition of every hypothesis. If the evidence supports the thesis, constrain the claim to the observed laboratory and tested configurations. Otherwise describe the unsupported distinction or measurement limitation. All empirical conclusions here remain pending.
5.4 Contributions to Knowledge

The intended contribution is a protocol that connects a graphical dependency model to matched collection, defender-side feature extraction, grouped validation and explicit robustness tests. A second intended contribution is a qualified dataset or restricted evidence package with actor provenance and controls. A third is a scope-qualified model/feature comparison. These remain prospective until collection, qualification and appropriate release are completed.

Prior work already addresses automation classes, AI-family fingerprints and shared-stimulus human–AI comparisons. The contribution is an extension in measurement and validation, not an asserted universal first. A well-supported negative result can clarify which apparent signatures fail when collection conditions are matched.
5.5 Limitations and Future Work

Future work should broaden independent participants, checkpoints, scaffolds and target networks and examine longitudinal drift. Vary hardware placement, prompts, skills and missing sensors systematically. Five-day laboratory scores should not be treated as deployment readiness. Operational evaluation requires external validation and realistic false-positive analysis.

More rows may not be the best investment. If performance improves mainly with new groups, collect diverse operators rather than repeated windows. If instrumentation dominates, repair it first. If a task creates a shortcut, rematch the task instead of adding model complexity. These decisions should follow learning curves and quality audits rather than a preferred hypothesis outcome.
